patterns.comment: `//` to the end of the line, and there is no block comment. `#` is not a comment in slate — it is only ever the shebang, and only on the first byte of the file.
patterns.name: comment.line.double-slash.slate

patterns.comment: A `#!` line is read at the very first byte and nowhere else. It belongs to the kernel rather than to the language, which is why it is scoped as a comment.
patterns.name: comment.line.number-sign.slate

patterns.comment: An interpolated string: `s"…"`, with `${expr}` and the bare `$name` short form. The prefix is scoped separately so the `s` reads as the operator it is rather than as part of the text.
patterns.name: string.quoted.double.interpolated.slate

patterns.comment: `$name` interpolates the name and stops there — a `.x` after it is text, which is why only the name itself is scoped.
patterns.name: meta.embedded.expression.slate

patterns.comment: `@test` and its neighbours. `@` also writes a binding pattern (`n @ number`), which is the form with whitespace around it and is left to the operator rule.
patterns.name: entity.name.function.decorator.slate

patterns.comment: A standard module is spelled `slate:name` and is one token to a reader — the whole of it is scoped, so `slate:http` does not read as a label followed by a name.
patterns.name: support.class.module.slate

patterns.comment: The soft words. `class`, `data`, `type` and `end` are not keywords — a program may still call something `end` — so each is recognised only where it introduces something, which is what stops `val end = 1` lighting up.
`end`, `from` and `proto` close a block, name a superclass and attach a prototype. All three are soft, so they are matched where they stand rather than everywhere.
patterns.name: keyword.control.slate

patterns.comment: The hard keywords, exactly as `word_kind` in the lexer has them. `end`, `class`, `data`, `type` and `from` are deliberately absent: they are soft words the parser decides by what follows.
patterns.name: keyword.control.slate

patterns.comment: The twenty-one words that test for a kind in pattern position, plus the type words an annotation uses. None of them is a keyword — `val date = readIt()` is an ordinary binding — so they are scoped as types rather than as control words, which is the difference a reader is being shown.
patterns.name: support.type.slate

patterns.comment: `_` where a value goes is the parameter of a function nobody wrote. It is scoped as a parameter for exactly that reason.
patterns.name: variable.parameter.placeholder.slate

patterns.comment: A closing tag: `` or ``. A capitalised name is a component and a lower-case one is a tag, which is the distinction the compiler itself draws.
An opening tag, up to its `>` or `/>`. Attribute values are ordinary strings, and a `{…}` attribute or child is an expression scoped by `$self`.

A name immediately before a `(` is being called. Written without a lookbehind for `.` so that a method call lights up the same way a free one does — `xs.map(f)` IS `map(xs, f)`, and the highlighting says so.
patterns.name: entity.name.function.slate
